newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices seen up in India, down in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices seen up in India, down in Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to firm in India due to thin supplies and fall in Pakistan owing to large supplies from farms in the next few days, dealers said on Thursday.
In India, cotton prices were firm last week on strong demand from fabric makers ahead of the Hindu festival season and on thin supplies with the season drawing to a close, traders said.
In spot deals Gujarat Kalyan rose 1,300-1,400 rupees to 14,000-14,200 per candy (355.56 kg) while Wagad cotton jumped 1,800-1,900 to 13,000 per candy.
Fears that new crop arrivals might be delayed in the Gujarat region in western India also pushed up prices, one broker said.
Trading in Punjab cotton was low, but prices looked up on the back of the rise in Gujarat varieties, he said.
Bengal-deshi in spot deals rose from 820-860 rupees to 875-900 per maund (37.32 kg) while October delivery was quoted higher at 940 rupees and November at 925 rupees per maund.
Reports that viral disease had hit the cotton crop in northern India also triggered some speculative interest during the week.
Cotton output in India during the 1995/96 season (September-August) is put at 15.70 million 170-kg bales.
"We were expecting a crop of 16/16.50 million bales for 1996/97 but there are some doubts after the reports of viral disease," one trader said.

In Pakistan, rates were likely to drop to 2,000 rupees per maund in the next few days due to increased supplies from farms to ginneries and higher availability to spinners, broker Nasim Usman at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
"Cotton rates dropped sharply in local markets on Thursday despite a sharp rise in New York following reports of a short crop in the United States," Usman said.
In the kerb market, rates for NIAB-78 fell to 2,275 from 2,375 on Tuesday, Usman said. The market was closed on Wednesday owing to a public holiday.
"There has been no impact of a sudden rise of cotton rates in New York in the Pakistani market," Usman said.
The main factor behind the slide was higher supplies from farms where the crop was good and expected to produce 11 million 375-lb bales, Usman said.
Omer Farooq Ehsan Chhani, vice-chairman of the Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association, says cotton production could reach 12.5 million bales.
The KCA said exports had reached 1.82 million 375-lb bales by August 25 since the 1995/96 season began on September 1, 1995.
